youtube.baslik: How the Ear Develops: Embryology of the Ear | Lesson 35 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
We explain how the ear develops before birth: the inner ear from the otic placode and otic vesicle, the middle ear from the first pharyngeal pouch, the ossicles from the pharyngeal arches, and the outer ear from the first cleft and six hillocks. We also look at microtia, atresia and inner ear malformations, and why hearing assessment matters in these infants.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Moore, Persaud and Torchia, The Developing Human: Clinically Oriented Embryology; Sadler, Langman's Medical Embryology; Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Sennaroğlu L and Saatçi I, A new classification for cochleovestibular malformations, Laryngoscope (2002).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Embryology of the inner, middle and outer ear
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how the ear develops in the womb, that is, the embryology of the ear.
We will see that the inner, middle and outer ear come from different origins, and how this explains congenital ear anomalies.
The three parts of the ear develop from separate places in the embryo and at different times, then join into a single organ.
The inner ear develops from a thickening of the ectoderm, the embryo's surface layer, and it is the first part to appear.
The middle ear cavity develops from the first pharyngeal pouch, and the ossicles from the first and second pharyngeal arches.
The ear canal develops from the first pharyngeal cleft, and the pinna from small hillocks on the first and second arches.
These different origins matter clinically: outer and middle ear anomalies often occur together, while the inner ear is often normal.
Now let us look at each part in turn.
To understand ear embryology, we first need to know the pharyngeal arches.
In the fourth and fifth weeks, a series of arches forms in the neck region of the embryo, seen from outside as ridges.
Each arch has its own cartilage, muscle, nerve and blood vessel.
Between the arches there are clefts on the outside and pouches on the inside; clefts are lined by ectoderm and pouches by endoderm.
The nerve of the first arch is the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve, and the nerve of the second arch is the facial nerve.
As we saw earlier, the tensor tympani works with the trigeminal nerve and the stapedius with the facial nerve; this origin is why.
The inner ear is the first part of the developing ear.
At the end of the third week, around day twenty two, a thickening of ectoderm appears on each side of the hindbrain: the otic placode.
The placode folds inward and forms the otic pit.
By the end of the fourth week, the mouth of the pit closes and a fluid-filled sac separates from the surface: the otic vesicle.
The otic vesicle is also called the otocyst; the entire membranous labyrinth develops from this small sac.
Cells that break away from the wall of the vesicle form the ganglion containing the nerve cells of the hearing and balance nerve.
This whole process takes place in the first month of pregnancy, often before the mother even knows she is pregnant.
The otic vesicle soon divides into two parts.
The upper, dorsal part gives rise to the utricle and the three semicircular canals.
The endolymphatic duct and sac also arise from this upper part.
The lower, ventral part gives rise to the saccule and the cochlear duct.
The semicircular canals appear in the sixth week as flat pouches; when the center of each pouch fuses and disappears, the canals form.
So the balance and hearing parts of the membranous labyrinth develop from the same sac and stay connected.
This connection explains why the inner ear is a single fluid system and why some diseases can affect both hearing and balance.

sahneler.baslik: The cochlea and the *organ of Corti*
cumleler: In the sixth week, a tube grows out from the lower end of the saccule and begins to coil: the cochlear duct.
By the end of the eighth week, the cochlear duct makes about two and a half turns and completes its snail shape.
The surrounding tissue turns first into cartilage and then into bone, forming the otic capsule that encloses the inner ear.
Over the next weeks, cells on the floor of the cochlear duct become hair cells and supporting cells, forming the organ of Corti.
The cochlea begins to function at around the twentieth week of pregnancy.
Studies in the second half of pregnancy have shown that the fetus responds to sound.
At birth the cochlea is adult size, but the higher parts of the auditory pathway keep maturing after birth.

sahneler.baslik: The first pouch: *the middle ear cavity*
cumleler: The middle ear cavity develops from the tubotympanic recess, formed as the first pharyngeal pouch lengthens.
The outer end of this recess widens to form the middle ear cavity, while the narrow inner part forms the Eustachian tube.
So the middle ear and the Eustachian tube are lined by a mucosa of the same origin as the lining of the throat.
Late in the fetal period, the cavity expands backward and forms the mastoid antrum.
The mastoid air cells develop after birth; this is called pneumatization.
This shared origin with the throat also helps us understand how nose and throat infections reach the middle ear.
The ossicles develop from the cartilages of the pharyngeal arches.
The malleus and incus develop mostly from Meckel's cartilage, the cartilage of the first arch.
The stapes develops mostly from Reichert's cartilage, the cartilage of the second arch.
Sources accept that the otic capsule also contributes to the inner-ear side of the stapes footplate.
For most of the fetal period, the ossicles stay embedded in loose connective tissue.
This tissue clears at about the eighth month, and the ossicles become free to vibrate in the air-filled space.
The muscles follow the same origin: the tensor tympani develops from the first arch and the stapedius from the second.
The tympanic membrane develops where the first pharyngeal cleft and the first pouch meet.
Its outer layer has the same origin as the skin of the ear canal, that is, ectoderm.
Its inner layer has the same origin as the middle ear mucosa, that is, endoderm.
The fibrous middle layer forms from the connective tissue between the two.
So the three-layer structure of the eardrum we saw in earlier lessons has its roots in embryology.
The ear canal develops from the dorsal part of the first pharyngeal cleft.
At the start of the third month, cells at the bottom of the cleft multiply and form a cell plug that blocks the canal.
This plug breaks down at about the seventh month, and the canal opens again.
If the canal does not open, or opens only partly, congenital aural atresia or canal stenosis results.
In atresia, sound cannot reach the eardrum, so there is a marked conductive hearing loss.
The loss is often around fifty to sixty decibels; if the inner ear is normal, bone conduction thresholds are also normal.

lejant.metin: Right air conduction: _55 to 60 dB HL_

cumleler: This sample audiogram shows the findings of a child with congenital aural atresia in the right ear.
Air conduction thresholds are between fifty five and sixty decibels, a typical conductive loss.
Masked bone conduction thresholds are within normal limits, so the inner ear is working.
The left ear is normal; in one-sided atresia, good hearing in the other ear is very important for language development.
Because bone conduction is normal, devices that deliver sound by bone conduction can be considered; we will see these in later lessons.

notlar.metin: Rises from the neck _to the side of the head_

cumleler: The pinna develops from six small hillocks that appear on the first and second pharyngeal arches around the sixth week.
Three hillocks lie on the first arch and three on the second; over time they merge to form the folds of the pinna.
As we saw earlier, small irregularities in this merging can lead to pits or skin tags in front of the ear.
The pinna starts out in the lower neck; as the lower jaw develops, it rises to the side of the head.
So in some syndromes, a pinna set lower than normal can be a clue to a problem in development.
The pinna keeps growing after birth and reaches adult size mostly during childhood.
A disruption in development leads to different anomalies depending on when and where it happens.
Microtia is a small, misshapen pinna; complete absence of the pinna is called anotia.
Microtia is often accompanied by aural atresia and ossicular anomalies.
In the middle ear, the ossicles may be fused, missing or immobile, which leads to a conductive loss.
Inner ear anomalies reflect an arrest of development at a certain stage; the earlier the arrest, the more severe the anomaly.
The most severe form is Michel aplasia, in which the inner ear does not develop at all.
The Mondini deformity, in which the cochlea does not complete its full two and a half turns, is another well-known example.
A widely used classification of inner ear anomalies comes from Sennaroğlu and colleagues at Hacettepe; we will see it in later lessons.
Some ear anomalies have genetic causes, and some arise from environmental factors during pregnancy.
For example, in Treacher Collins syndrome, outer and middle ear anomalies occur together with differences in the facial bones.
The first three months of pregnancy are when the organs form, so this is the period most sensitive to outside factors.
Rubella infection during this period can affect the inner ear, which is why vaccination is so important.
Some drugs can also disrupt ear development in pregnancy; for example, some retinoic acid drugs can cause microtia.
The timing of development determines which structure is affected, and this explains how anomalies tend to occur together.
Now let us bring this development together on a timeline; the weeks are approximate.
The inner ear begins in the third week, and the cochlea completes its two and a half turns by the end of the eighth week.
The cochlea begins to function at around the twentieth week.
The middle ear begins from the first pouch in the fourth week; the ossicles become free at about the eighth month.
The pinna begins to form from the hillocks in the sixth week; the ear canal is plugged in the third month and opens again in the seventh.
This timeline helps us think about which structure can be affected at which stage of pregnancy.

sahneler.metin: In an infant with a pinna or canal anomaly, assess the inner ear separately: bone conduction ABR shows cochlear function. Always test the normal-looking ear too.
cumleler: A useful tip for the clinic: in an infant with an anomaly of the pinna or ear canal, do not judge hearing by appearance.
Even if the outer and middle ear are affected, the inner ear is often normal; only bone conduction testing can show this.
In infants, this assessment is usually done with the bone conduction auditory brainstem response, or ABR.
The other ear, even if it looks normal, must always be tested too; in some children both ears are affected.
The inner ear starts from the otic placode at the end of week three and grows from the otic vesicle; the cochlea is coiled by week eight.
The middle ear develops from the first pharyngeal pouch; the malleus and incus come from the first arch, and the stapes from the second.
The ear canal develops from the first pharyngeal cleft, and the pinna from six hillocks on two arches.
Because their origins differ, the inner ear is often normal in microtia and atresia.

sahneler.soru: Where does the stapes mostly develop from?
sahneler.aciklama: The stapes develops mostly from Reichert's cartilage of the _second arch_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: from which embryonic structure does the stapes mostly develop?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the second pharyngeal arch, that is, Reichert's cartilage.
The malleus and incus, in contrast, develop mostly from the first arch.
